newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia stocks end mixed, Philippine stocks soar.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks end mixed, Philippine stocks soar.

text.p: Asia stocks ended mixed on Friday as many regional currency markets were rattled after the Philippines became the second Southeast Asian county to effectively devalue its currency in just over a week.
Philippine stocks staged the largest, single-day rise in four years on the news, while other Southeast Asia markets weakened.
Elsewhere, Hong Kong stocks rallied in a largely technical rebound, while those in Tokyo closed higher.
On July 2, Thailand effectively devalued the baht by 15 percent, sending jitters through Asian centres as speculation mounted over who would be next.
The authorities in the Philippines have spent the past week strenuously denying they would devalue the peso and sold hundreds of millions of dollars to support the currency.
But on Friday the central bank announced it would widen the currency's trading band in a move it said was aimed at ridding the market of speculators.
The peso fell more than 11 percent following the news to a low of 29.45 to the dollar before the Bankers Association of the Philippines halted peso/dollar onshore trading for the day.
However, Philippine stocks soared, with the main share index rising 189.99 points, or 7.57 percent, to close at 2701.14.
President Fidel Ramos defended the move as necessary to preserve the country's economic gains and called the central bank's move a "decisive action".
In Washington, IMF managing director Michel Camdessus applauded the Philippine action as one that would protect the economy from instability in regional financial markets.
"It eased the tension among investors in the equities market," said Cora Guidote, head of Philippine equities at UBS Securities (East Asia) Ltd.
Bankers criticized the Philippine central bank, saying it had lost its credibility by seeming to contradict earlier statements on its foreign exchange policy.
But businessmen welcomed the change as inevitable and said it would relieve businesses of the burden of the high interest rates that were needed to bolster the currency.
As the ripple effect spread through currency markets, local stock markets initially fell victim to some of the jitters before recovering.

In Malaysia the key index fell below 1,000 to a new 1-1/2 year low of 988.47 points before recovering on what some dealers said appeared to be government intervention. The key index ended 9.09 points, or 0.90 percent, higher at 1,017.61.
Dealers said the market remained nervous despite repeated assurances by the central bank that it would defend the ringgit.
After opening stronger, Thai stocks were battered as the baht dived and investors worried about how much listed firms' would incur in foreign exchange losses.
"The baht's further weakness would result in higher foreign exchange loss of most companies than previously expected," one broker said.
The baht fell to a record low of around 29.90/30.00 per dollar onshore in mid-morning trade on a spillover effect from the Philippine peso's slump.
The SET index plunged 20.78 points, or 3.20 percent to close at 628.55.
Stocks in Singapore ended off 1.20 points, or 0.06 percent, at 1,967.14 as the budget was being delivered.
Heavy selling in PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Telkom) had dragged the market lower from the opening and pushed it down over one percent near the close before it recovered slightly.

The stock had lost 5/8 in New York overnight to close at 33-3/8 and fell 175 rupiah in Jakarta on Friday to 3,925 rupiah. The Jakarta stock exchange index fell to a day's low of 721.33 before recovering slightly to end 5.74 points, or 0.79 percent, lower, at 723.42.
Late on Friday, the Indonesian central bank said it widened its intervention band for the rupiah to 12 percent from eight percent, which had little impact on stocks.
The Hang Seng Index was up 386.06 points, or 2.60 percent, at 15,225.29.
Tokyo shares recovered earlier losses brought on by concern over troubles in Japan's financial sector.
The key Nikkei 225-share index ended 120.71 points, or 0.61 percent, at 19,840.
Buying of small-cap stocks helped pull South Korean stocks slightly higher, leaving the index up 0.53 of a point at 768.30 at the close.
Taiwan shares fell on profit-taking, with the index ending down 35.11 points, or 0.37 percent, at 9,394.63. Earlier, it had risen to 9,526.74, a seven-year intraday high.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index finished 4.7 points, or 0.17 percent, at 2,699.1, while New Zealand shares closed 9.64 points higher at 2,516.84.
